title: Acute Rash Assessment
summary: A clinician-facing prompt for assessing acute rash, recognising life-threatening infectious and drug reactions, distinguishing serious causes from benign viral exanthems, and supporting safe triage and urgent referral.

sections.title: Assessment priorities
sections.intro: Use this guide as a prompt. It does not replace clinical judgement, specialist assessment or urgent escalation when serious pathology is suspected.

items.title: Must confirm or exclude
mustConfirmOrExclude: Meningococcal septicaemia (non-blanching petechial rash, fever, systemic illness, meningeal signs).
Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis (mucosal involvement, blistering, skin necrosis).
Severe drug reaction or anaphylaxis (angioedema, breathing difficulty, hypotension, recent drug exposure).
Infectious exanthem requiring isolation (measles, chickenpox, scarlet fever, herpes zoster).
Cellulitis or other spreading soft-tissue infection (localised warmth, swelling, systemic illness).
Severe systemic illness with rash (sepsis, toxic shock syndrome).
Immunosuppression increasing infection risk or unusual presentation risk.
items.importantLimitation: Absence of meningeal signs does not exclude meningococcal disease. Early rash may not be petechial or non-blanching.

sections.title: Focused history
sections.intro: Characterise rash onset, distribution and associated symptoms to guide diagnosis.

items.title: Rash characteristics and distribution
mustConfirmOrExclude: Onset: sudden vs. gradual; duration; progression pattern.
Distribution: localised vs. generalised; symmetrical or asymmetrical; areas of predilection.
Morphology: maculae, papules, vesicles, pustules, blisters, petechiae, purpura.
Blanching: does it blanch with pressure? (petechial rash that does NOT blanch is ominous).
Associated: itch, pain, fever, systemic symptoms.

items.title: Systemic and constitutional features
mustConfirmOrExclude: Fever, rigors, chills or night sweats.
Malaise, fatigue, myalgia, headache or sore throat.
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or abdominal pain.
Breathing difficulty, throat tightness or wheeze (anaphylaxis).
Recent upper-respiratory infection or sick contacts.

items.title: Red-flag features in history
mustConfirmOrExclude: Non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash with fever (meningococcal).
Mucosal involvement: mouth ulcers, lip swelling, eye involvement.
Blistering, skin peeling or necrosis (Stevens-Johnson, TEN).
Recent new drug (antibiotics, NSAIDs, anticonvulsants most common).
Signs of anaphylaxis: throat tightness, breathing difficulty, hypotension, angioedema.
Spreading localised redness (cellulitis).
Known immunosuppression or HIV.

sections.title: Serious pathology screen
sections.intro: Positive features should trigger urgent ED referral or same-day specialist assessment.

items.title: Meningococcal septicaemia
urgentFeatures: Non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash (often on trunk, lower limbs, pressure areas).
Fever with systemic illness, meningeal signs or altered consciousness.
Rapid progression; may develop shock.
Rash typically appears 12-24 hours after fever onset.
implications: Immediate emergency referral and empiric antibiotics (do not delay for lumbar puncture).

items.title: Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis
urgentFeatures: Facial oedema, mucosal erosions (mouth, eyes, genitals).
Widespread blistering or skin necrosis.
Recent new drug (antibiotics, NSAIDs, anticonvulsants).
Fever, malaise and systemic involvement.
implications: Immediate hospital referral for specialist dermatology and intensive care.

items.title: Anaphylaxis
urgentFeatures: Urticarial rash with angioedema (face, lips, airway).
Throat tightness, breathing difficulty or stridor.
Hypotension, shock or reduced consciousness.
Recent drug exposure, food or insect sting.
implications: Immediate intramuscular adrenaline and emergency assessment.

items.title: Serious infectious exanthem
urgentFeatures: Measles, chickenpox or scarlet fever in vulnerable populations (pregnancy, immunosuppression).
Severe systemic illness with exanthem.
Complications: encephalitis, myocarditis, secondary infection.
implications: Hospital assessment and infection control precautions.

sections.title: Focused examination
sections.intro: Examine for rash characteristics, distribution and signs of systemic illness.

items.title: General appearance and vital signs
howToTest: Assess consciousness, orientation and signs of systemic illness.
Record temperature, heart rate, blood pressure and respiratory rate.
Note any signs of shock: pallor, cold extremities, delayed capillary refill.
normal: Alert, haemodynamically stable, normal temperature or low-grade fever.
abnormal: Altered consciousness, fever >38.5°C, tachycardia, hypotension or signs of shock.
implications: Systemic illness with rash suggests serious infection or drug reaction.

items.title: Rash morphology and distribution
howToTest: Document exact location, extent and spread pattern.
Describe morphology: macules, papules, vesicles, pustules, petechiae, purpura, blisters.
TEST FOR BLANCHING: press with glass tumbler; petechial rash that does NOT blanch is red flag.
Note any mucosal involvement (mouth, conjunctivae, genitals).
Assess for secondary infection or crusting.
normal: Blanching erythema or papules; no vesicles or purpura; no mucosal involvement.
abnormal: Non-blanching petechiae or purpura; vesicles or blisters; mucosal ulcers; necrosis.
implications: Non-blanching purpura suggests meningococcaemia; vesicles suggest varicella or herpes; mucosal involvement suggests serious drug reaction.

items.title: Meningeal signs
howToTest: Test neck stiffness, Kernig sign and Brudzinski sign (see Acute Headache assessment).
Assess for petechial rash distribution on trunk, legs and pressure areas.
normal: No neck stiffness, negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
abnormal: Neck stiffness, positive Kernig or Brudzinski sign, petechial rash with fever.
implications: Meningeal signs with petechial rash = meningococcal septicaemia; emergency referral.

sections.title: Common clinical patterns
sections.intro: Pattern recognition supports diagnosis but does not replace serious pathology screening.

items.title: Viral exanthem
commonFindings: Maculopapular rash following viral prodrome (fever, cough, coryza).
Rash appears 3-5 days after fever onset.
Blanching erythema; no vesicles or purpura.
implications: Supportive care; no specific treatment needed.

items.title: Chickenpox (varicella zoster)
commonFindings: Vesicular rash in crops; clear fluid then crusting.
Crops appear over 3-5 days; 'all stages' appearance.
Contact isolation needed; isolation until all vesicles crusted.
implications: Supportive care; antivirals if immunocompromised or severe. Avoid contact with vulnerable groups.

items.title: Drug reaction (maculopapular)
commonFindings: Rash 3-7 days after new drug (antibiotics, NSAIDs most common).
implications: Discontinue causative drug; supportive care; antihistamines if itchy.

items.title: Cellulitis
commonFindings: Often follows break in skin (wound, insect bite, athlete's foot).
implications: Antibiotic therapy indicated; monitor for spreading or systemic deterioration.

sections.title: Management and disposition
sections.intro: Base decisions on serious pathology assessment and urgency of referral.

items.title: Community management is appropriate when
mustConfirmOrExclude: No red-flag features for serious pathology present.
Rash is blanching; no petechiae or purpura.
No mucosal involvement.
Likely diagnosis is viral exanthem, uncomplicated varicella or benign drug reaction.
Patient well with manageable fever.

items.title: Urgent ED referral (same-day or emergency)
urgentFeatures: Non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash with fever (meningococcal).
Blistering, skin necrosis or mucosal involvement (Stevens-Johnson/TEN).
Angioedema, breathing difficulty or signs of anaphylaxis.
Spreading cellulitis with systemic illness.
Severe systemic illness with rash (sepsis, shock).
implications: Emergency or same-day hospital assessment required.

items.title: Acute rash
safetyNetting: Call 999 or go to ED immediately for: non-blanching petechial rash with fever; difficulty breathing or throat tightness (anaphylaxis); blistering or skin peeling; spreading rash with severe systemic illness; or signs of shock.

Contact your GP or go to ED same-day for: widespread rash with fever; mucosal ulcers or eye involvement; rash with meningeal signs; localised rapidly spreading redness (cellulitis); or new rash after starting a medication.
Speak to your GP if: rash is not improving after 1 week; rash is spreading; you develop new symptoms; or you want advice about infection risk to others.
